cards.reviewerHold: Two faults, both in text no ruling has touched. Everything else is sound. (1) The definition 'you can see straight through it' is a CLAUSE, not a definition of an adjective. It is the same fault I held trivial for in round 2 ('it hardly matters at all' is a clause, not a definition of an adjective), which was fixed in V2. Publishing this one would apply the rule to one card and not the next. The LIVE T3 adjective exemplars are phrases ('very puzzled', 'strange in a spooky way', 'so bright it is hard to look at', 'without much strength'). Fix: 'see-through, so you can see what is on the other side', or 'letting light through, so you can see what is behind it'. Avoid 'glass' because it is a distractor on bank-vr-04-closest-meaning-35, the reasoning the drafter rightly applied to 'small' on trivial. (2) The image prompt 'A clear plastic lunchbox on a table with a leaking sandwich visible inside.' would illustrate something a child cannot make sense of: a sandwich does not leak, and a leaking one reads as mess rather than see-through. It also illustrates a different scene from the card's own sentence. Fix: 'A clear stream flowing over smooth pebbles, with every pebble visible through the water.' That matches the sentence and shows the meaning directly. Sound and unchanged: the sentence 'The stream was so transparent we could count the pebbles.' is one sentence, British, child-suitable, and fixes the see-through sense without ambiguity. Word class adjective is right. Tier 3 sits with dazzling, eerie, genuine and feeble among the T3 exemplars, as I found in R1054. One-sense is right, matching my round-1 view and David's R1057. The card agrees with the key 'clear' on both LIVE items (gen-38 at T3, bank-35 at T3), and none of their distractors (thin, shiny, obvious, opaque, glass, window) becomes correct under it. No ruling is needed: both fixes are redrafts of free text, and neither touches the tier, the sense count or likelierKnown.
